The Annales Historici, maintained by the Dvorak Elves of Lusia, is a history and geography of the known world: languages, cultures, economies, political structures, habits of trade and governance from the western sea to the eastern limits of what can be verified. Merchants and princes pay generously for fine editions. It is among the few works in this list whose value is straightforward. Your Grace will note that many of these works are most useful not for what they contain, but for what others believe they contain, or are compelled to perform belief in. I do not include these out of vanity; intellectual authority is a powerful force in Singhapura, and thus in all its dominions. Not for nothing do are the lands beyond its borders ridiculed as barbarians and unsophisticated. To Your Grace, therefore, I give not chores, but new weapons.

107.title: Of Singhapura, the Great Empire
107.content: The poet Additya Wickrama was a man of considerable gifts and considerable debts, the latter of which he resolved by dying. He once wrote thus: there are two kinds of people: those who belong to Singhapura, and those who will. He owed me six hundred and thirty-eight Owls at the time, which colors my affection for the observation, but I have traveled widely and I have not found reason to dispute it. Singhapura is the greatest continuous Empire in the known world. It is the largest political, economic, and military power of our age. It stands at the forefront of infrastructure, education, magical development, and industrial capacity. It sprawls from the Diamond River Delta through the Balalpura Plains, one of the world’s great breadbaskets, to the Raavanskandha Mountains, said to be the bones of the dead god Raavan. It continues up into the mountain fastnesses of Udanuwara and Giridhora, past the Hooniyang Pass, from where it controls Wattle and Daub. To the south, it holds the entire coastline and the thousand islands of Tangowan as a vassal state. Singhapura is the primary political fact of Your Grace’s governance. Fortunately, I am well-versed in its nature, having spent a greater part of my years therein; allow me, therefore, to guide Your Grace at length on the subject.

108.title: Of the City, Which Is Also the Empire
108.content: To understand Singhapura the empire, one must first understand Singhapura, the heart-city of the empire. The city was originally founded at the Diamond River delta, and then moved piecemeal and rebuilt in the shadow of the Raavanskandha mountains. All roads lead to Singhapura, or so it is said. Indeed, follow any road from any end of the empire; follow the lion statues - follow the Diamond River, monsoon-waters so wide you cannot see the end, and then at the end are vast Balalpura Plains, a sea of green interspersed by great chasming moats that shine crimson, as if watered with blood. This is Rathmada Samudra, more than five thousand hectares of reservoirs running red with Taprobane-cultivated algae, built to enrich and irrigate the land; beyond it, at the foot of the Raavanskansha mountains, is a vast city, fronted by great bridges. Your Grace, standing at the bridges, will see a great number of peoples and homes and buildings even before the city walls, which rise higher and higher as one goes in, until at the very apex sit several great towers. Inside the walls is a world of glass and metal and spires, the hum of waterworks and arcane machinery, roads worth more than diamonds. The city is organized in concentric rings representing the cosmic order. At the center is Adhiraj House, built by the Lusian architect Andretto d’Orenzo alongside the finest mages of Taprobane; here lie the Adhiraj’s quarters and all essential administration, and the towers one can see with the naked eye. Below are the Botanical Gardens - the entire known world in microcosm, every plant from every place the empire can reach, trade with, or control. In the rings below are the sprawling buildings of the Taprobane Imperial University, the greatest university in the world, from which magic was and continues to be revolutionized; the offices of the Red and White Councils of the Haugris Church, and all its attendants; at the very bottom, by the great roads, come merchant, unloading cargo onto great runic conveyors. From Tangowan, from Wattle, from Lusia, from the Rosantic League, even from lands further still - all flock here. The water infrastructure alone, built in these mountain lands, represents an administrative and engineering achievement that most states could not conceive. If Your Grace sees vast roots of stone, like a great hand laid upon the city, know that this is the Mahabag Subha, its underground and overground canals connecting public tanks across the entire breadth of the city, some extending hundreds of miles to supply entire towns. The Sunken Church sits behind the city and above it; carved into the foothills of the Raavanskandha, it houses what the Haugris Church holds to be the Divine Corpus: the preserved remains of Raavan himself. It is a holy place, drawing pilgrims from the city in a ceaseless grey stream. The Ruins of Vidyaakara lie visible in the plains to the east, restored by the Temple of Eighteen. They are said to be one of the oldest remnants of ancient Samarskand - a stupas, a university, monasteries, with sealed areas yet unexplored, about the size of Daub; it should tell you much that the Empire is thus able to preserve an entire city thus, unused, for the sake of historical curiosity and antiquity. There are, of course, satellite cities, as large but perhaps not as storied. Nagenapura to the East, Basnapura to the West, Ruhunapura to the South; and in between a thousand towns and minor dealings, all the way up to Udunuwara and Giridhora, which guard the passage to the North. Your Grace will not deal with these satellite cities directly. As Duchess of Daub, Your Grace is technically above most administrators and provincial nobility encountered on the road south; this is a pitfall, and I will urge you caution. Anything said in such conversations will be met with smiles and hospitality but little else, and promptly reported to Singhapura; conversely, little of import will be said unless by one specifically authorized to do so by the center.

109.title: Of How the Empire Is Actually Governed
109.content: Political theorists - I invoke Weerasingha and his student Molligoda, the latter of which I will spare Your Grace - have long since attempted to build classifications of empires in the same way that Taprobane classified magicians. One may use their thinking to describe Singhapura accurately as a divine-right absolute unitary state. Unfortunately, one may describe it equally accurately as an aristocratic legal feudal state with federal characteristics, and still be correct. This is the problem with applying theory to practice. Your Grace should understand that the empire’s apparent monolithic unity, as seen from Daub, is the face it presents to its periphery. Firstly, Singhapura nobility, Your Grace, is unusual. It is the custom around the world that noble title be drawn from some holding of land and people. In Singhapura one can live in a mud hut or a small city tenement and still be ennobled, either for some great work of scholarship, or of art, or some valorous deed in service of the state. Various Adhirajs, have, at times, bestowed land; but it is customary now for ennoblement to come with a fee commensurate to the deed rendered, paid annually. Indeed, the Grandmaster and Paragon ranks of magicians of the Taprobane Imperial University carry with them the priviledges of ennoblement. Onwership of land is now held to be the right of the state and the state alone; estates that are mismanaged can be given to others, or parcelled out, or taken over for public works. There are fixed rules about manners of crests and customs, of address, and even of weapons; for example, unless otherwise bestowed by the Adhiraj, a member of a noble family may only carry on their person one kasthane, a curved blade, worn as a signifier of rank; though often highly decorated with lion motifs and even gems and the like, the actual blade is kept short, so that it may hang no further than the length of a coat. Hereditary power is real but not absolute - it can be stripped by the Adhiraj, the Church, or the judgment of peers. A commoner from a remote province can acquire a crest with the right patronage and the right deeds to their name. The bureaucracy, is appointed by and answerable to the Adhiraj, a system of Justice of Peace and Low and High Courts in each territory; these are, indeed, nobles, but it is the appointment that gives them power, not their nobility. Thus, Your Grace, the nobility of Singhapura are not its primary power, however great their wealth may seem. It is best understood as a merchant-military aristocracy in which the Empire positions useful people and their families. In reality, at the summit of the Empire sit four entities: the Singha Adhiraj, the Haugris Church, the Taprobane University, and the Guilds. They are four great powers in permanent negotiation, each dependent on the others, each limiting the others, each seeking advantage over the others. The Adhiraj is the Highest of the High - First Prophet of the Haugris Church, Judge and Arbiter Above All, High Commander of all military forces. His word is law. In theory, he exercises total control over every aspect of the empire. In practice, everyday authority is delegated and wielded by others, while the Adhiraj crafts law, oversees the greatest of strategy and public works, and reserves supreme authority for moments that require it. The position is not hereditary; the Adhiraj selects a successor from the nobility and adopts them as heir. Theoretically, this position is open to anyone who demonstrates sufficient skill; in practice, the Ministers of the Interior, Trade, and Justice are commonly the chief candidates. The question of succession is thus permanently open and permanently political. The Haugris Church handles the empire’s messaging and controls large portions of its money, education, and health. Its internal structure runs through Red and White Councils. The White Council dictates internal policy and major judgments; the Red oversees regional appointments and logistics. Underneath these Councils are three Sequences that form the body of the Church, and a fourth that does not get discussed in polite company. The Sequence of Letters runs the mail network and is, underneath that function, the most sophisticated intelligence operation ever constructed; the Sequence of Discourse produces the bureaucrats who go on to become the administrative functions of the Church; the Sequence of Acts produces the public face: priests, healers, diplomats, explorers. The Samanera Corps is the fourth; it was the Church’s answer, in its time, to orders like the Paladins, and is a great deal more violent and capable. These four sequences are the Empire’s public presence in most of its outlying territories, including Your Grace’s own. The Taprobane University theoretically exists outside the political structure. Practically, the people who devise and control the most powerful magic in the known world are involved in every aspect of Singhapura’s development. After all, the Taprobane system of magic, which is modern Ritualism, is the empire’s decisive advantage in every domain in which it operates. The University trains not only magicians but lawyers, judges, and engineers; thus it has sway even in places nominally outside its fiefdom, from the architects of the well-to-do to the most rural of courts. Its friendly rivalry with the Lesser Theoretical University of Daub is, from the University’s perspective, intellectual sport conducted with a lesser rival that serves a common cause. Last but not the least are the Guilds. It should not surprise one to learn that those who make the products of empire have a great sway over it. These forces I would not underestimate; it is well-said that while the sword of the Adhiraj are the Military Orders, the arrows are the Guilds. The Guilds hold no formal legal authority except over themselves, but in reality they exercise considerable practical power over everything; by far the greatest is the Singhapura Merchants Guild, which is both trading-house and bank with private armies and navies attached. Your Grace may see in this the dangers of this model for the Daub and Wattle Guilds. The ideals behind the Empire are real: universal law, the Taprobane system, free education, centralized administration, competitive examination for almost every post, heavy investment in new technologies. However, what holds it together is a shared calculation; that this arrangement is more practical than any available alternative, and that together they are stronger than any of them would be alone.

110.title: Of the Empire’s Tensions and Opportunities Therein
110.content: No structure this large is without strain, and I would be failing Your Grace’s interests if I catalogued Singhapura’s strengths without attending to what lies beneath them. The first is steel. The empire requires high-quality steel - for construction, for armies, for everything that holds a civilization together. Centuries of exploitation have depleted the accessible metal deposits of Udanuwara. The empire is pushing north again, which is why the trade relationships through Wattle and Daub matter more now than they did a generation ago. It also means that whoever controls northern trade routes has both leverage and a noose around their own necks. This, more than any, is why Singhapura desires control over Wattle. Your Grace should be aware of what flows through Daub, and what that flow is worth to the Empire. The second is religious. The Haugris Church dominates, but the Temple of Eighteen remains powerful in the eastern provinces, and the Iron Pagoda grows in the southwest. The Taprobane University increasingly chafes at the Church’s involvement in magical regulation. These pressures, one suspects, are held carefully by the Singha Adhiraj, lest one incumbent prove too powerful. Daub has both the Church and the Temple within its walls. Your Grace manages this as a local equilibrium, but it is also a microcosm of a larger war of faiths and reason. The third is the frontier. The empire’s particular frontiers are consequential. There is Wattle and Daub to the north, and the Waste beyond them. Tangowan to the south. Lusia and the Rosantic League to the west; and many Tears around the border cities due to magical excess. A wise empire must watch its borders. The Military Orders are a consistent drain on resources here, a condition that worsens as the supply of metals tightens.

111.title: Of the Governance of Daub, and What It Means to Stand in the Shadow of the Empire
111.content: This brings us to Daub. Your Grace governs a city and province that is too well-positioned to ignore. However, if I may make so bold, the arrangement - tribute, nominal deference, and the occasional imperial quest - is a softer noose than one may expect in such circumstances, especially when Wattle struggles beneath tighter bonds. It may very well be that the Adhiraj is content to let Daub exist and grow as a vassal; it may also be that the fruit is being ripened for the picking. My belief, however, is that the Empire, and especially its Guilds, desire trade with provinces beyond - the Obsidian Empire, for one; and that having observed Lusia, and the advantages of having a free port in the north. There are three direct avenues I would urge Your Grace to examine. The Military Orders of Singhapura exist in uneasy tension with Your Grace’s Charter Knights, the Paladins, and whatever mercenaries are present at any given moment. These Orders have trained for war against the north; that is their present orientation and capability. The Church is in subtle but tense dialogue with the Temple across Daub’s wards and provinces. The Merchants Guild will trade and intermingle whether or not it is invited to; from here come the strings of capital, favors, and votes. I will not advise Your Grace on how to deal with the Adhiraj directly. What I will say is this: the empire, for all its coherence and capability, is a machine built by human hands, maintained by human institutions, and subject to the tides that affect any large human enterprise. It may present a unified face to its periphery, but Your Grace has the advantage of being close enough to see behind that face, and experienced enough to decide which aspects of it you wish to see in your own mirror.

112.title: Further Reading
112.content: A ruler who wishes to understand Singhapura must first understand that it produces, in abundance, the means by which it prefers to be understood. Your Grace will find this pattern familiar. It is not unique among states, but Singhapura has been more systematic about it than most, so much so that every major ward and province has its own censor, whose duty it is to inspect materials before publication; even plays and literature are examined thus. The same Additya Wickrama that I spoke of earlier was fond of musing that the most dangerous thing anyone can do is believe the Empire’s account of itself; such words would never have been allowed to be distributed in writing in Singhapura. Indeed, my own writing herein is protected partly by censorial precedent (I have not stated anything that does not have some record in the public eye) but partly also by dint of this law not applying to Daub or such outlying provinces. Even so, if this work is to be read in Singhapura, it must either be given special accord by the Taprobane University, circulated internally for its own uses; or it must be edited to suit the tastes of censors. With this stated plainly, let me recommend some additional works. The Singha Chronicle is the official account of the founding and the history of the Singhapura Empire. For Your Grace, it will be most instructive; not only in its account of how the Empire wishes to be seen, but it also contains the most complete record available of approved crests and sigils, and for this reason alone it remains indispensable in any dispute concerning lineage or the legitimacy of claims. I have compresssed the histories into a more readable account of my own devising in other chapters. The Himakatu Chronicle covers the affairs of the North that the Singha Chronicle prefers to pass over quickly. It concerns the building of Himakatupura and the failures of Empress Kudakaali II that led to the daemon breakthrough and the ultimate creation of the Great Northern Waste. It is a tragedy in every sense, full of glory, hubris, violence and power; it is the Empire at its worst, and in some sense may explain the shame that the Empire, even today, sees lingering in the ruins of Wattle. The Ithihaasa Potha is a sequence of epic poems composed by seventeen philosopher-poets once exiled from Singhapura. It is the only known work of prophecy that has consistently proven accurate. Every prediction has thus far been fulfilled, but in the most indirect and perverse manner imaginable. I recommend it to Your Grace not because it contains a map of the future - indeed, its lines are often so vague and allusive as to be hopelessly incomprehensible even to scholars of literature; but because of the hold it has on the minds of those who govern. Indeed, to a great degree, it may be said to be behind the Empire’s tacit obsession with horoscopes and astrology, which may not govern its armies, but do indeed have a great play in the dates for marraiges and the breaking of ground for works of all kinds. The Assembly of Gold and Saffron, maintained by the Haugris Church, is assigned to schoolchildren throughout Church territories. It is, by the consensus of everyone compelled to read it, among the most tedious documents in any tradition. Nevertheless, it is vital in understanding how the Church sees itself. In its pages are recorded the minutae of almost every decision made by the Church, down to minutes of the Red and White Councils. The Reflections of the Moon in Still Water, attributed to the Nameless Sage of the Temple of Eighteen, is a collection of verse in the manner of aphorism set to poetry. Its primary social function is the conferral of apparent profundity. A ruler who can produce a passage at the right moment will be taken for a person steeped in the customs of the Temple, whether she is one or not. This I trust Your Grace may put to use. Lastly, there is Weerasingha’s foundational analysis on the arrangement of states, extended by Molligoda. It reduces all states to three basic forms and subdivides each by the source of its legitimacy, the scope of its power, and the structure through which that power operates. I will spare Your Grace the need to read Molligoda, a man universally recognized for his singular lack of talent in the art of letters; I have summarized its salient contents elswehere in this work.

114.title: Of Tangowan
114.content: Tangowan lies far to the south, and its commerce reaches Daub only at several removes. I include it here not because Your Grace will have much occasion to deal with it directly, but because it is the clearest available demonstration of what Singhapura may do to a place unchecked. Wattle and Daub are but partial incorporations; the Empire’s hand is shown rather than felt; Tangowan, with no armies and no great industry, is the fullest expression of power.

115.title: Of What Tangowan Is and Was
115.content: Tangowan is an archipelago. In size it is vast: thousands of islands, dense jungles, volcanic mountains, and monsoons, spread across a territory almost as large as the entire North. Its natural wealth is extraordinary. Daub must labor for its crops and Singhapura must engineer its water, but Tangowan simply produces - rarewoods, fisheries, spices, wild game; it is said one can assemble a decent meal simply by strolling around in the morning. The sea yields to its fishermen and divers with a generosity that has no equivalent elsewhere in the known world. The people of Tangowan named their lands the Sagarika Mandalam. The approximate rendering of this is “the Realm of the Ocean”; we call them Tangowan, which derives from a translation error made by the diplomat Vanarkali in the seventh century. It is the latter name that the world now knows them by; that it rests on a mistake, and that the mistake has never been corrected and never will be, will tell Your Grace much. Before Singhapura, governance rested with a council of nineteen governors called the Paridarakas. These rulers were selected by lot, numbering in their dominion a major island or cluster of smaller ones. Periodically, it is said, a Paradarika would call for a Maha Sabha, or a gathering, to resolve great matters. Outside the Sabha, each administered their domain as an independent body with its own customs. Laws were not written down, but customs arose owing to need and circumstance, and disputes were resolved in accordance with the community, especially its elders. In this we see, Your Grace, no great sophistication, but the mechanisms similar to a family governing itself. The failure of such a system in the face of Singhapura is most instructive. The Paridarakas had authority over small lots; but none had the capacity to set forth coordinated ideals, a shared goal, and to arm all of Tangowan under pressure. In times of peace and plenty ordinary people might collect and share resources as needed, but wars require a grim purpose and an authority that cannot be dissuaded by the winds of opinion and fear. When Singhapura arrived, there was no single throat to cut; there instead were nineteen fragments, each with their own interests. Even where individual rulers opposed Singhapura, there were always some great part of the community that could be swayed, and the Paridarakas who opposed were eventually cast aside by their own people. The economy compounded this effect. Tangowan is known for its kula; these are family artisan clans whose techniques were passed down through the generations. They were capable of intricate and extraordinary craft - even today, Tangowan craftsmen produce some of the finest carvings and most elaborate of seaworthy vessels. But on the whole, this system also produced extraordinary insularity: to one born outside the right families, there was little to do. Talented young people with aptitudes for engineering or large-scale organization drifted toward Singhapura. From this, and from the flight of the alchemists in Lusia, we gain a great lesson: talents in poorly organized places always drift toward wherever organization exists.

116.title: Of the Singhapura Merchants Guild And Its Acts
116.content: Here I wish for Your Grace’s particular attention, because this is where Tangowan’s incorporation becomes most instructive for Daub. The lord who enters a territory with an army has announced his intentions and provoked resistance. However, the merchant who arrives with goods and services, especially ones that existing institutions, cannot provide is instead greeted by benevolence, and even love, until such time as they are indespensible. Thus it was with Singhapura Merchants Guild. At first they came for crafts; then, having convinced others of the profits of such trade, the Guild systematically moved into everything outside the protected traditional crafts. Singhapura metals and jewellery and silks became items of great value. Tangowan had no immediate need for grain, but the Merchants sold it cheap, and complimented it with such spices and tea as are ruinously expensive to grow except in very large estates. Such actions decimated what little existed of Tangowan farming. It was more profitable for a man who spend some hours idly whittling, and to trade a minor token of carving for a sack of rice, than to spent hours laboriously weeding his crops. Having thus enticed the populace, the Merchants set about acquiring land. There are records of Tangowan governors handing over vast acres in exchange for a pittance: a hundred swords here, or furnishings for a mansion there. For without an economy, or an authority that understood it, the value of land was utterly unrealized. On these lands they began growing tea, pepper, cloves, nutmeg, saffron, fruits, cotton and such others as Singhapura needed; and this embraced with enthusiasm by much of Tangowan. At this point there was no existing commercial infrastructure to resist Singhapura: the kula system had no mechanism for operating at scale; the rulers had no banks and no organized trade beyond their individual arrangements; when the Guild arrived with credit and supply chains and the organizational capacity to turn Tangowan’s natural wealth into reliable exportable income, it was seen as a great opportunity. Soon the Merchants Guild held dominion over large tracts of Tangowan. The rulers who accommodated it earliest did best in the short term. That this was also the mechanism of their demise became clear only in retrospect. It only remained for the Adhiraj to issue but one command, and all of Tangowan, having already surrendered their lives, fell to their knees. This is not a novel pattern. The history of Singhapura is full of kingdoms both new and old that have fallen in this manner; Ratnapura, Ridheepura, Balalpura, Udunuwara, Giridhora - these entries are recorded proudly in the Singha Chronicles, and great care is taken to mention that they profited from the arrangement. But I may note, your Grace, that of Ratnapura and many others, only their names remain. There are no great histories of their works save for a few scattered legends and minor works of poetry and theater. One day the name Sagarika Mandalam, too, will be a footnote thus, an object reserved for entertainments and little else. Your Grace has a Merchants Guild in Daub, modelled closely after its cousin in Singhapura. I do not say this to alarm; in this, Your Grace has a natural defense; in fact, it may be bold to allow it to flourish even more in directions that Your Grace decides, such that the mechanisms of selfish economic interests are allied to the protection of your state. Without it, the tale of Tangowan becomes an omen for the subjugation of other kingdoms. As the philosophers say: history does not repeat itself, but it often rhymes.

117.title: Of the Church’s Intrusions
117.content: The Haugris Church is now building schools and hospitals across Tangowan. I wish to dwell on this. Schools and hospitals are often recieved as an instrument of benevolence; but they are far more. Consider what a school does, Your Grace. It takes children at the age when the world is still being explained to them. The children educated in Church schools will learn the Singhapura account of history, of legitimacy, of what constitutes proper governance and proper devotion. They will not remember the Tangowan Maha Sabha as a living institution. They will know it, if they know it at all, as a thing their grandparents clung on to, some sort of primitive and naive notion that was rightfully dispelled by the civilizations of the Emprie. The memory of the old order does not need to be suppressed; it merely needs to be seen as archaic, a matter for history-books which bore children. Thus a new order is securely established. A people so educated, even if they rise in rebellion, can only replicate such mechanisms as the Empire has given to them. Hospitals work similarly. A population that receives its medical care from the Church is a population with a reason to think well of the Church. The care is genuine; the people who staff these institutions believe fully in the virtue of what they do; however, gratitude is a form of loyalty, and loyalty established at such individual levels, on visible bodies, is remarkably durable, especially when no such thing has existed before. Thus any new order must face the question of how to provide this service that the public now firmly believe is their lot. The Haugris Church is building schools and hospitals in Daub as well. Your Grace has thus far managed the Church as befits a religious and military faction; however, I wish to draw your deliberate attention to these other enterprises. The moment any institution becomes the only source of something a population cannot do without, that institution has acquired a form of power that political authority cannot easily check. Tangowan had nothing to replace the Church with; Your Grace should be clear-eyed about preventing a similar situation occurring in Daub.

118.title: Of Tangowan Religion and Spirits
118.content: It is an interesting feature of Tangowan that it has not wholly embraced the Church and the worship of Great Raavan. In fact it may said to be the only form of rebellion left. Tangowan worship has centered on two classes of being: the Yami, powerful and unpredictable nature spirits inhabiting ancient trees, rivers, volcanoes, and the like, requiring appeasement through offerings and ritual; and the Uso, ancestral household spirits protecting family and hearth, honored through daily domestic practice. Most Tangowan people worship as many Yami as their circumstances require, without the exclusive affiliations that characterize Temple or Church devotion. Indeed, many have adopted Raavan as yet another Yami to appease, and continue to go about their daily lives unbothered. Some scholars have proposed that this represents a hybrid of deity worship and a form of ascendancy similar to the Rosantic Ascended. The scholarship is less important than the existence of this one resiliency. This we may attribute to culture rather than institution. I note that it is not resistance, but more along the old adage: the bamboo bends with the wind, but does not break. In extraordinary circumstances, this, too, may be a form of power. The empire has been wise enough, thus far, not to attempt a direct reorganization of this state of affairs. I note that it has become fashionable among Singhapura’s nobility to vacation in Tangowan for purposes of spiritual communion. The Yami are not, from what the accounts suggest, beings who respond well to aristocratic tourism; nevertheless, such income appears to be greatly raising the living standards of certain groups on the coast, in the same manner that certain villages of Daub benefit from tourism. I leave the matter there.

119.title: Of Tangowan’s Errors, Stated Plainly for Daub’s Benefit
119.content: A Duchesss who wishes to learn from another’s misfortune should be able to name the errors precisely. Your Grace will naturally see more than I do; I shall make my list here. The first error was the structure of the Maha Sabha, and of its weaknesses when such the time came to act collectively against an external power. Your Grace’s own council arrangements should be examined with this in mind. The question is not whether they function under ordinary conditions but whether they would function under extraordinary pressures. The second error was the export of talent.A territory that exports its most capable people is, in a meaningful sense, financing its own death. Tangowan’s best minds became artisans and engineers and administrators in Singhapura; they were of no service to their home, and with good reason. Your Grace has a partial answer to this problem in the form of the Lesser Taprobane University, but it alone cannot make up the deficit of citizens in the ruralities who lack for any gainful employment. The third error was the absence of redundancy. Every essential admistrative function in Tangowan was performed either by a single family or the ruler thus appointed. A system with redundancy may be said to be bloated, but a system with no redundancy has no resilience; remove any single piece and the whole shatters. This principle I extend from my studies and practice of magic and Ritual.In this regard, the overlapping complexity of Daub’s institutional landscape may be an asset, provided it is sculpted by a careful hand to extend beyond mere factionalism. Competing institutions drain resources, but they also present a bulwark against the weakness of a single load-bearing pillar. The fourth error, which contains all the others, was the confusion of natural wealth with strength. Tangowan was rich, but riches alone are not strength. Strength is the organized capacity to defend a state. Daub, too, is rich, and has some strength: Your Grace’s networks, the Charter Knights, the LTU, and the Merchants Guild’s roots go deep in this ground; and yet there is no strength that can give an empire pause. This, Your Grace, is worth considering.

120.title: Further Reading
120.content: For the incorporation of Tangowan under Singhapura rule, the Singha Chronicle devotes one paragraph to the event. The Annales Historici, however, devotes forty pages; thus the scholarship of the Dvorak Elves recommends itself again to us. Tangowan Straits is a novel about a captain’s obsession, set in the archipelago. Its account of the spirit geography - the Yami, their invocations, their jurisdictions - is perhaps the only written account of these rites. That the most reliable account of this subject available is a novel is a tragedy, but it seems the truth must sometimes be buried in lies to survive.

122.title: Of Transit and Intelligence
122.content: The workings that follow concern themselves with distance: crossings, contractions, and the transmission of intelligence across it. Your Grace may demand these of her practitioners; as a caution, may I urge Your Grace to be aware of those same practitioners who may hold such capabilities without her oversight. Timmet’s Threshold of the World, also known as Timmet’s First . Transports the caster’s astral body or soul, the distinction remaining genuinely unclear, to a transitional realm for formal congress with daemons. This became possible with the consent of daemons after the success of the first Sin-Eater Legion. Entry and exit are tightly governed; the Ritual will not activate unless a counterpart on the other side consents to the intrusion. It is a cheap working, but for most practitioners it does nothing at all, for a reason Your Grace will appreciate in politics: you must know people before you can get through the door. Timmet’s Hall of Ten Thousand Turnings, also known as Timmet’s Second . Transports the caster to a second transitional realm between planes. Unlike the first Ritual, this one leads a series of endless hallways and rooms, each leading off from the others, containing no air and no water. It is suspected to either be an abandoned realm; enquiries with knowledgeable daemons have resulted in signs that say SITE UNDER CONSTRUCTION on the doors. There are traces of older civilisations in the form of artefacts and partial structures of unknown origin. Survival requires continuous energy expenditure. Some believe that these are remnants of the Graveyard Sutra residue from extremely large, extremely old magic, possibly from Samarskand. The cost of this Ritual is continuous and very high; there is a specialised division at Taprobane University called the Halldivers that treats this as their professional domain. Timmet’s Exchange of Equal Masses, also known as Timmet’s Third . Teleports the caster by swapping their mass with an equivalent volume of material at the destination. The cost formula is distance squared multiplied by mass squared, which makes long-range use ruinous. The preparation required is considerable; the Ritual is used primarily in heavy construction and military operations, where the logistics justify the expense. It also requires the careful calibration of masses - for reasons yet unknown, when the position of the swap is tightly specified, the volume of material involved becomes impossible to define; when the material is too clearly defined, its subsequent position is impossible to calculate. The Taprobane university requires magicians who would use this spell to attend classes on legal scholarship and courtroom argument. Nandamitra’s Mother . The most widely used long-distance communication Ritual in the corpus, named not for its creator but for the opening words of the original test message: my mother wants to know if you are coming for dinner. The mechanism is another Ritual called Gajaba’s Thread, reworked so as to apply to speech. It creates a thread between two points, with speech travelling in both directions by mutual consent, and the cost of magic is borne equally between both parties. A long conversation over a great distance is therefore a shared expense. Its weakness is that this connection is difficult to make private without other Rituals of obfuscation and decryption. The signal, as we call it, travels through whatever natural conductors exist between the two points; in cities, the workings of the Iron Sutra forces it along trees, stray animals, and sometimes even people. There is a Ritual called an Intercept and another called The Man in The Middle that has been designed specifically to catch this signal and enable a third to deceive both parties. Your Grace’s advisors, if tempted to rely on this Ritual, should avoid it at all costs for sensitive communications. Malavika’s Distant Witness . Detaches a portion of the caster’s sensory awareness and projects it forward as an invisible observer, capable of perceiving sight and sound at the location it occupies. It travels by the Water Sutra’s principles and cannot be rushed or compelled; it finds the most available path, which is not always the most direct one, and cannot pass through complete barriers of worked stone or dense metal. Its military utility is considerable and it is widely employed. Taprobane-trained scouts regard it as standard equipment. The failure mode Your Grace must understand is this: the Witness is the caster’s actual awareness. The caster’s body remains behind, insensate and entirely undefended, for the duration. If the Witness is detected and destroyed - by Volta’s Lantern, by a practitioner skilled enough to seize and collapse it - the caster suffers the equivalent of a severe blow and may be incapacitated for some days afterward. Experienced scouts do not use it alone. Your Grace should never permit a practitioner to deploy this Ritual without a physical guard posted at their body; to do otherwise is to leave a trained asset lying helpless on the ground while their mind is elsewhere. Gajaba’s Leash . A development of Gajaba’s Thread, adapted for purposes of tracking rather than connection. Where the original Thread links separated parts of a single entity, the Leash attaches one end of a Thread to a specific person or object, established through physical contact at the time of casting, and allows the holder of the other end to sense the location and general condition of the target at will. It is the standard instrument of Singhapura’s Charter Knights when pursuing fugitives, and is in regular use by the intelligence for the monitoring of persons of interest. The critical limitation is one learned at considerable expense, and which Your Grace should hold firmly in mind: the Thread is bidirectional. A person of any meaningful magical sensitivity will, in time, become aware that they are being tracked. A trained practitioner can follow the Thread back to its source. The Leash therefore cannot be concealed. It can be cut cleanly by Sapumal’s Sundering, and other workings can even send Rituals back along the Leash to the origin; which is why Singhapura’s courts now specify in their warrants that multiple Leashes be attached at all times to subjects in prison. Patali’s Whisper . Encodes a short message - the practical limit is a few spoken sentences - into a physical object or a person’s body, for retrieval at a later time by touch or by the utterance of a specified phrase. Unlike Nandamitra’s Mother, the message is stored rather than transmitted; there is no signal to intercept. It is used extensively in dead drops, for sealed orders, and others. The Iron Sutra governs which materials will hold a Whisper reliably. Organic materials - seasoned wood, worked leather, human bone - retain it cleanly for days or weeks. Alloys hold it poorly; a Whisper encoded in iron or bronze often decays within hours. Encoding in a living carrier is peculiarly difficult. Kanaka’s Mirror . A continuous passive Ritual that alerts the caster when their person or location is subjected to magical observation, tracking, or scrying. It operates through Mirror Sutra principles: the practitioner’s understanding of their own magical presence becomes sensitive to any intrusion upon it. It is standard equipment for high-value diplomatic missions out of Singhapura, and a matter of professional habit for any practitioner who has, in the course of their career, accumulated enemies of sufficient competence. The irony is that Kanaka’s Mirror is itself perfectly visible. Any practitioner running Volta’s Lantern will see it as clearly as a lamp in a dark room. It announces that the person carrying it has something worth protecting and expects surveillance. A ruler’s ambassador who arrives wearing Kanaka’s Mirror has told the host court something before she has opened her mouth. The more sophisticated approach is to run the Mirror intermittently, on a schedule irregular enough to provide genuine warning without providing a permanent beacon. The discipline this requires is, in practice, considerable. Mahendra’s Decoy . Creates a false magical signature at a specified location: the convincing appearance of a practitioner at work, an active Ritual in progress, or an accumulation of magical residue suggesting recent and significant workings. The Decoy can be set to mimic whichever class of signature the caster specifies. Military applications range from drawing enemy scouts toward empty ground to persuading an adversary’s magical analysts that a force is positioned elsewhere, or that a fortification has been more or less heavily worked than it has. It is maintained at a continuous energy cost proportional to the complexity of what is being imitated. The Heart Sutra is the binding constraint; the Decoy must be narratively plausible to sustain itself. Volta’s Lantern, in particular, is adept at breaking weak Decoys that make no sense in context. Taprobane doctrine as an examination topic is that the most effective Decoys are those that are completely plausible. The analyst’s eye, having found one real thing, extends a measure of trust to what surrounds it. This principle, Your Grace will observe, is not unique to magic.

125.title: Of Wattle, Its Governance, and the Nature of Your Grace’s Position Within It
125.content: To understand Wattle, one must first set aside the image that Singhapura’s theaters have made so profitable: the doom-haunted heroes, feuding lords, and the fell winds of winter. These are useful fictions, and I shall return to their utility. The reality beneath them is a kingdom of considerable size and import, surviving the attentions of an empire not through military valor, but through a combination of geographic awkwardness and the particular genius of its present king. Wattle is a large kingdom. Lesser Wattle alone, the great agricultural basin that constitutes its southern reach, feeds a significant portion of the North: Ealdorfold draws on its grain in lean years, as do the border territories, and Daub has more than once found itself grateful for Wattle’s harvest. The Waste adds to this a stranger form of wealth: Wattle sits at the world’s most accessible border with the Waste, and the artefacts its Wastewalkers bring back are in Queensgate at prices that would embarrass many a Lusian banker. To its ports flock buyers and sellers from the Rosantic League, and with them come wealth, books, and mercenaries; through it, to Giridhora and Udunuwara, goes the trade from Ealdorfold that the Empire so greatly desires. Himakatupura, the northernmost city of the Empire, was originally built as a profitable fort-city, positioned to extend the empire’s reach and to service Ealdorfold’s appetite for Singhapura grain, cloth, and fine goods. Wattle is built on those ruins, more completely than Daub. Much of what governs it today is the accumulated residue of repurposement, and on its shoulders it bears the strain of the Empire, which, having made it a vassal, will not idly relinquish its old ambitions. Your Grace answers nominally to Wattle and through Wattle to the Empire, but this holds only insofar as Wattle can stand between Daub and Singhapura’s direct attention. In that task it has proven, historically, to be a poor wall. I state this plainly not to diminish Wattle but because a clear-eyed account of its condition is necessary. A commander whose shelter is ill-understood is one whose surprises are deeply unpleasant to those who follow.

126.title: Of What Wattle Is
126.content: Greater Wattle is not a city in the ordinary sense, but a province that, put together, contains more souls than the three principal cities of the Rosantic League combined; an analogue from the South would be the combined population of Singhapura and Basnapura. Its construction was piecemeal and its reconstruction frequent; the result is a sprawling and fragmented set of districts, each a seat of some power. Centuries of Northern, Rosantic and Lusian immigration have produced an equally fragmented culture and an economy that Singhapura theorists often regards with exasperation. It does not make much sense, but on the whole it works together; though why it does not fall apart, and what should replace it, is the subject of many a tavern discussion. The Crown Quarter occupies the repurposed remnants of the Palaces of Himakatupura, built where the river Sut meets the sea. Here sits King Allant’s palace and Antler Hall, where ambassadors are received and feast-courts held; the Chancery, which manages correspondence with Singhapura; the Tower of the Constable, which houses the royal garrison; and the port. This port is an arterial lever of power: whomsoever controls the port controls the Crown Quarter controls the port, and thus the wealth that flows in and out of Wattle. We suspect the Crown Quarter also contains the former site of the torture chambers of the infamous Empress Kudakaali II. They may yet be there. There is also the Round Tiltyard, capable of holding six thousand spectators, commissioned by Allant’s predecessor Aneirin to host the annual Tournament of the Table of Lords. This theater is an important political stage; knights fight for glory under heraldric banners, and the Great Houses, who fund the prize armaments, compete for reputation. Overlooking this field is the Singhapura consulate: the Empire’s eye on King Allant and his dominion. Hauterive, at a slight remove, is the fief of many lords and ladies of the Great Houses. It is rich with heavily guarded townhouses; the nobility maintain estates elsewhere and use these for matters of politics in the city. The Pendragons maintain a fortified townhouse that predates Allant’s reign by generations; House Carpenter’s hall has its own forge. The Table of Lords used to meet here before Allant removed such discussions to the Crown Quarter; many, of course, say that nothing has changed in reality. Rubble, out of sight of Hauterive, houses most of Wattle’s poor and many of its immigrants. There is still old Himakatupura stonework in the foundations. The Haugris Church maintains its most significant building here - a basilica serving as hospital and grain-dole house. The Rubble Night Market thrives without royal license. They say anything that can be bought and sold will be found here. Crowgarden, built later and outside the older districts, contains the mills, bakeries, market gardens, fullers, and tanneries, and has little defense. Its Crowgarden Common serves as an overflow tournament field. The breadbasket of Lesser Wattle surrounds it; its edges touch the Waste. Queensgate, across the river, is the market district proper: the Grain Exchange, the cloth halls, the money-changers, and the factor-houses of the Wattle Merchants Guild, alongside Lusian and Rosantic consulates. The Wastewalkers’ Exchange operates here; it is where Waste salvage is assayed, licensed, and sold to buyers from near and afar. Here, too, is another artery of trade, for this is where the Twilight Road ends. Thus, goods from Daub; goods from Ealdorfold; goods from Sinhapura; all things eventually come through here. The Gontreach lies well to the north, and contains great ruins. From these emerge the Temple of Eighteen’s new monastery complex; around it have accumulated hedge-wizard descendants of banished magicians, the dwellings of much of Wattle scholars, magicians; here, too, are Rosantic sorcerors fleeing their lands, Lusian alchemists searching for secrets and better prospects, and many who study the waste. At its far edge is the Keeper’s Gate, said to once have been a fort at the furthest edge of Himakatupura domain; now all that remains is toll-arch over the road to that section of the Waste that divides Wattle from the boundaries of Ealdorfold. Nominally this is Crown territory, but in practice it is left to the Wastewalkers, who collect no tolls and will only turn away children who stray too far.

127.title: Of King Allant and His Position
127.content: Allant was not born to the throne of Wattle. The third son of a minor lord of no great name, his story would have been much like others, if not for his talents in war, and the rarer talent of making men loyal to him. Your Grace knows this chapter of his history well: Allant spent the better part of two decades as a mercenary captain, building from nothing the company that would become known as the Dukes of the North. It is my understanding - and this Your Grace will know better than I do - that the North, in those early years, was in crisis. Aneirin the Bard-King’s death had produced a generation of petty conflicts and excesses; one only needs to peruse the stories of Pendragon Cador, Pendragon Loholt, or Igraine the Elder; though petty cheftains to the Empire, their immediate power must have been terrible to those crushed under their heels. Allant is remembered by the commons of Wattle as the man who came out of that chaos and ended it: who, with his faithful band, protected villages that the Great Houses had stripped for provisions; who broke many an unjust warlord; who, despite many a fault, became the king the times needed him to be, and ultimately unified Greater Wattle and thus the North. Lesser seen is the entry point of Allant into Singhapura’s political calculations. The Pendragons, House Carpenter, and three other Great Houses had spent themselves against each other; Allant arrived with an intact army and made himself useful to the Chancery as a man who could explain Wattle’s many squabbles to Singhapura, and who could be trusted on to protect critical trade interests. Thus, with enough of the Merchants Guild’s confidence, Allant earned, perhaps not outright approval, but the Empire’s willingness to bargain with the one seemingly sane sword in the North. The transition was not bloodless; again, Your Grace would know this side of history better than anyone else. The Pendragons did not accept this situation gracefully, and for a while there was great furor under Valerius the Ironhand. What followed was a twofold humiliation - the armies of Singhapura sweeping aside the main Pendragon force, and later years of slow public disrepute; despite ceremonies and the public clasping of hands, the Pendragons found themselves on the losing side of disputes entirely unrelated to the succession - debts, contested contracts, great losses in trade, land disputes, uprisings, and general disrepute. These latter events are better ascribed to Allant than to Singhapura. Your Grace will note that I have not mentioned her own position in this history; not from ignorance, but as Allant’s former lieutenant, Your Grace understands her deeds and rewards better than I can say. What can be said is that of the record I have been able to examine, Allant brings to mind the Lusian general Septimus and his epitaph: No friend has ever served me whom I did not treat with gold; no enemy has ever wronged me whom I did not repay with ashes. Thus all accounts are settled. Allant’s present rule is sometimes mistaken for that of moderate. However, if I may make so bold: Allant has not grown out of his warmonger days, but merely tempered himself. His security lies in the management of competing interests, each positioned such that they stand to gain from his existence and lose from his absence. He treats simultaneously with Singhapura, the Merchants Guild, the Great Houses, the Temple, Lusian money, Rosantic ambitions, and Ealdorfold interests; all are held in precarious balance, maintained by the studied impression that Allant is, to each of them, the indispensable man. He is regarded with genuine warmth by the commons and the lesser houses, who see in him a man of no grand birth who saved the North in its time of need. He is regarded with caution and respect by the Great Houses, who remember the Pendragons and their very public fall. It is commonly held that a ruler must choose between being loved and being feared, since the two rarely coexist. Allant has, I believe,amply demonstrated that this is not always the case. There is, however, a vulnerability in this foundation that time will eventually expose. The Dukes of the North - the company of those such as Your Grace, or Jerem the Red, are now a generation older; their children are of a different disposition. The quality of loyalty forged in war is different to that forged in peace and plenty. Allant understands this; it is, I suspect, one of the reasons he has invested so heavily in the Concordant College and the arrangements with the Merchants Guild; but the transition from personal authority to institutional authority is as yet incomplete. The Great Houses remain a threat. The Pendragons are a powerful call to older times; House Carpenter holds enormous tracts of land and industry. The old aristocracy - Wulfstane, Clavering, Hollow, Pelhamor, Gautierre, Garlande, Balaain, Morgaunt - constitute the Table of Lords, and much of their power has followed Allant’s attentions into the commercial, migrating from the militaric to the Wattle Merchants Guild. This places Wattle’s greatest concentration of wealth outside the hands of its ruler. We must speak of the Concordant College: King Allant’s intended rival to Taprobane and the LTU, drawing sorcerers and alchemists from Lusia and those whom Taprobane has declined to retain, focused on studying and reworking Waste artifacts. The Great Houses, who have begun to understand what a fully realized College would mean for the balance of power, are not pleased; nor is the Taprobane University, and thus Singhapura. It has not yet become what Allant intends; but Your Grace should watch it carefully. The LTU and Taprobane maintain a friendly rivalry because they were ultimately created by the same state. A Concordant College that achieves its ambitions will alter that equilibrium in unexpected manner. One further observation: a king who rose by making himself useful to Singhapura is a king the Empire believes, in some recess of its thinking, that it might easily replace. I cannot say if King Allant understands this. A wise ruler would build institutions rather than relying on his own person - but Allant competes with Table of Lords and sets them against each other than drawing them into functioning parts of a working whole. Your Grace may draw from this example whatever lessons seem applicable to Daub.

128.title: Of the Temple and the Church
128.content: The Haugris Church has a considerable name in Wattle, but little of it is good. The Temple of Eighteen is now the true devotional power; the Church has been reduced to a presence and a grain-dole. This inversion is extraordinarily unorthodox. Some ascribe this to the deliberate hand of the Adhiraj in this arrangement. I will, however, point to several other factors within Wattle. Firstly, there lies the Wattle tradition in which nobles are responsible for the education of those who live in their lands, which hamstrings the Church’s attempts at education. Secondly, the Temple of Eighteen is owed much in these lands. It is said that the Litanies of the Temple, appearing before battlefields, kept many great atrocities at bay in the days of old; it is also more practical to say that much of the knowledge of the Vedics and of the magicians of the North have been preserved by the Temple, and parcelled out according to their gifts. I may also point to the ready availability of Lusian capital for Temple purposes, and the reconstruction of the ruins in the Gontreach. Thus it is that the Eighteen are said to sit in the highest councils in Wattle, as they do in Lusia; with one hand they stave off the Haugris Church, and with the other prevent Wattle from going to war with itself. It may follow that this is then how certain houses have been able to rebuild despite a period of war, and how Wattle has, despite the enormous sums required, ever increased in glory. If Wattle is a battleground of faiths; it appears that for now the Empire has chosen to lose. In this I cannot help but remark on a skilled general who channels the enemy’s forces to one direction, such that they may win victories elsewhere.

129.title: Of Tourism and the Great Northern Romance
129.content: Wattle draws considerable tourism from Singhapura, and Daub by extension benefits from this in hidden ways. Let us leave aside the question of money and examine culture. The Great Northern Romance is a genre in Singhapura; Your Grace may recognize much of it as pure fantasy; but it is both sufficiently familiar to be legible and sufficiently foreign to be enormously compelling. The result is a Singhapura public with a sentimental investment in Wattle remaining what it is. Conservative factions within the Empire, who argue against fuller integration, find themselves opposed thus not only by practical arguments, but by a broad popular preference from the people of the same Empire that wishes to integrate it. Thus Wattle gains a resilience that extends well beyond the fortunes of King Allant or the current disposition of lords. Daub’s own share in this is not negligible; so long as Singhapura believes in what the North represents, that belief performs some portion of the work of walls and armies. Writers and poets are, owing to the difficulties of a career in the Arts, considerably cheaper than armies and arrows; and yet the ballads of Robert Holdbrook, Bloody Ygrain, and others travel further, and are sung with much gusto even among those who have the power to erase them from this world. Culture, again, reveals itself as a form of power; fictions endure; they are cheap, and difficult to attack without appearing ridiculous.

130.title: Further Reading
130.content: The founding and fall of Himakatupura are treated in depth in the Himakatu Chronicle. The Singha Chronicle also covers the same period, albeit too briefly. It is a general rule that those who commission histories do so in order to be well regarded by them, and neither departs from this rule; one records Kudakaali II’s many mistakes in generous beds of praise, and the other moves past, averting its eyes, attaching to her name all the faults of the Empire, so that it may be reborn on the opposite pages. Your Grace may find it more instructive to see instead how Singhapura sees Wattle. My first recommendation is the play Ganelon and Naimon, of which I have been an ardent supporter; its author is unknown, but it is very popular in Singhapura. It is a tragedy set around two brothers, both Paladins, who take unbreakable oaths and end on opposing sides; both brothers are dead by the end of the fourth act, the fifth act being an extended lament by the surviving company that later became a popular dirge. It almost single-handedly birthed the genre of the Great Northern Romance. Angenga is worth mentioning. It is a recent work set in the Concordant College and the Waste. A magician of great talent creates artificial life from smuggled Tungolstaana ore from Ealdorfold and the raw energies of the Waste: the Angenga, a being of immense strength and intelligence. The novel is then as much the Angenga’s story as Vikram’s - a created thing pursuing its creator across the Waste, driven by the torment of its own solitary existence. Its portrait of the College as a house of free inquiry, untethered from morality or political sentiment, is probably not accurate, but speaks to how the College is viewed outside Wattle.
